title: The School of Numbers at the Edge of Empire

title_i18n.en: The School of Numbers at the Edge of Empire

subtitle: At the frontier of Devagiri’s power, a grandson carves a house for numbers into stone
era: Transmission of Bhaskara II's mathematics in Yadava territory, c. 1185-1260 CE
region: Vijjalavida or Patan in Khandesh, Devagiri's scholarly hinterland
moral: Knowledge lasts when a society builds places to teach it.

sources.note: Primary epigraphic source for Bhaskara II's family and a school for his writings.

sources.citation: Bhaskara II, Siddhanta Shiromani and Karana-kutuhala
sources.note: Primary mathematical and astronomical works transmitted in the region.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009); David Pingree, 'Bhaskara II,' Dictionary of Scientific Biography (1970)
sources.note: Modern scholarship on Bhaskara II, Vijjalavida and textual transmission.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of an old stone slab half-buried in scrub, with faint Nagari letters, under a vast Deccan sky

dialogue.text: In the shadow of Devagiri, Bhaskara II’s grandson, Changadeva of Vijjalavida, carved a school of numbers into stone while empires shifted around him.

panels.shot: epic bird’s-eye over the Deccan plateau, with Devagiri fort in mid-distance and a small riverside settlement in the foreground

dialogue.text: Around 1207, the Yadavas ruled from rising Devagiri, yet far from the court a quieter work unfolded in the scrublands of Khandesh, in a place scholars call Vijjalavida.

panels.shot: slow push-in on an elderly Bhaskara II teaching under a tree, with a boy Changadeva watching

dialogue.text: Bhaskara, born in Vijjalavida, had written the Siddhanta Shiromani and Karana-kutuhala, works of sky and number; his family absorbed this learning like breath.

panels.shot: close-up on Bhaskara II’s hand writing on a palm leaf, faint stars sketched beside numbers

dialogue.text: In these leaves he set rules for eclipses and planetary paths, methods for algebra and arithmetic, verses that married verse and calculation in one breath.

panels.shot: medium shot of now-grown Changadeva in a modest house, holding an old manuscript with reverence

dialogue.text: By Changadeva’s time, his grandfather was gone, but the manuscripts remained—fragile, hand-copied threads linking their house to centuries of Indian astronomy and mathematics.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder of Changadeva reading by lamplight as rain lashes outside

dialogue.speaker: changadeva_and_bhaskara_ii
dialogue.text: If these verses stay only in this house, they will die with me.

panels.shot: wide shot of a small assembly of villagers and students before a shrine, with Changadeva addressing them

dialogue.text: The Changadeva inscription tells us he did more than memorize; he gathered land, people and purpose to make a place where Bhaskara’s works would be studied.

panels.shot: medium shot of a scribe chiseling letters into a stone slab while Changadeva dictates

dialogue.text: His charter, carved in stone, records a gift: land set aside so that students might live and learn, studying the Siddhanta Shiromani and Karana-kutuhala in this frontier village.

panels.shot: close-up on the carved inscription lines, with key words subtly emphasized by light

dialogue.text: Modern scholars reading this stone hear a clear voice: a grandson naming his lineage, naming Bhaskara’s texts, and tying their study to this soil.

panels.shot: interior wide of the new math school—a simple hall with students and diagrams

dialogue.text: This was no royal academy; the inscription names no king as founder. It shows a more common story—local initiative, family tradition, and quiet institutional work at the edge of empire.

panels.shot: medium shot of Changadeva teaching a verse, students chanting in unison

dialogue.text: Verses on sines, eclipses and arithmetic were chanted aloud. Memory carried the rules, while the school’s manuscripts carried their exact words into another generation.

panels.shot: close-up on a young student’s face lit by lamplight, reflected in his eye are star positions on a board

dialogue.speaker: changadeva_and_bhaskara_ii
dialogue.text: Remember: the verse is the key, the computation is the door it opens.

panels.shot: wide shot showing Devagiri fort in the distance as a caravan passes by the village school

dialogue.text: While Yadava power swelled and roads filled with caravans and soldiers, this small school quietly bound Vijjalavida’s past to Devagiri’s rising present through shared calculation.

panels.shot: medium shot of Changadeva and a visiting scholar exchanging manuscripts

dialogue.text: Texts did not stay still. Carried by scholars and students, copies of Bhaskara’s treatises travelled between such schools, weaving a network far beyond any single court.

panels.shot: documentary-style map overlay showing Maharashtra and Khandesh with a question mark at Vijjalavida

dialogue.text: Today we cannot place Vijjalavida with certainty; scholars debate its exact spot, though most see it in this Maharashtra–Khandesh belt, near the Yadava heartland.

panels.shot: split-panel feel: on one side, Changadeva teaching; on the other, a modern scholar reading the inscription

dialogue.text: Yet the inscription’s words are clear enough to bridge eight centuries, aligning the voices of Bhaskara’s house with those who read his verses today.

panels.shot: close-up on the weathered inscription now, with lichen on the stone and faint letters

dialogue.text: Kim Plofker and David Pingree read in this stone not a legend, but firm evidence of how Bhaskara’s works were kept alive in Yadava-country institutions.

panels.shot: slow pull-back from the stone to reveal ruins of the school and distant modern fields

dialogue.text: The later Kerala school would craft new techniques elsewhere, but this stone belongs to another story—of a Deccan lineage building a school so that inherited knowledge could outlast its founders.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot of a modern classroom overlaid faintly with silhouettes of Changadeva’s school

dialogue.text: Changadeva’s inscription reminds us that ideas endure not only through genius, but through places built to teach them—houses of number at the edge of empire, and in every age after.
